faq.a: No; common causes include Graves disease, multinodular goitre, Hashimoto thyroiditis, drugs (e.g., lithium) and infections.
faq.q: Is every goitre due to iodine deficiency?

faq.a: Yes; most multinodular goitres are euthyroid, but periodic testing is needed.
faq.q: Can a patient have a large goitre and be clinically euthyroid?

faq.a: For compressive symptoms, suspicion of cancer, or a rapidly growing nodule despite medical therapy.

exam: A 28‑year‑old farmer presents with a diffuse neck swelling and tremor. What is your next step and why? — Check TSH to differentiate Graves disease from simple iodine‑deficiency goitre; treat hyperthyroidism if TSH suppressed.

A patient with a 5 cm nodular goitre has normal TSH. How do you assess cancer risk without ultrasound? — Perform FNAC if the nodule is >1 cm or has suspicious features; if FNAC unavailable, refer for surgical opinion.

During a ward round you notice a patient with a goitre and new‑onset hoarseness. What does this indicate and what action is required? — Possible recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement or compression; arrange urgent airway assessment and ENT review.

In a region with endemic iodine deficiency, a child presents with a small goitre and normal thyroid function. What public health measure would you recommend? — Iodine supplementation through iodised salt or community fortification.

A pregnant woman develops a rapidly enlarging goitre. Which investigation is safest and what are management priorities? — Ultrasound (no radiation) to assess nodule; monitor thyroid function and treat hypo‑ or hyper‑thyroidism to protect mother and fetus.

You suspect thyroiditis in a patient with painful goitre and fever, but CRP is unavailable. How do you proceed? — Rely on clinical signs (tenderness, warmth) and consider empirical NSAIDs; if worsening, arrange drainage for suppurative infection.

A patient on lithium presents with a diffuse goitre. What is the mechanism and how should you manage it? — Lithium interferes with thyroid hormone synthesis causing goitre; review lithium need, consider dose reduction or switch, and monitor TSH.

Explain why a low‑resource hospital might prioritize a bedside thyroid exam over laboratory tests in an acute setting. — Immediate assessment of size, bruit and compressive signs guides urgent interventions when labs are delayed.
ai.title: Goitre
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Enlargement of the thyroid gland with varied causes. In low‑resource settings iodine deficiency, infections and goitrogenic drugs are common. Assessment focuses on size, function and red‑flag features.

b: Diffuse goitre → often functional (e.g., Graves, iodine deficiency)
Nodular goitre → risk of malignancy, usually euthyroid
sections.p: Goitre is any palpable enlargement of the thyroid. It may be diffuse or nodular and can be euthyroid, hyper‑ or hypothyroid. In East Africa iodine deficiency remains the leading cause, but infection, autoimmune disease and drug exposure are also frequent.

b: History: diet, family thyroid disease, radiation, drug exposure, symptoms of hypo‑/hyper‑thyroidism
Examination: assess symmetry, consistency, bruit, eye signs, skin changes
sections.p: Diagnosing goitre requires a systematic history, focused neck exam and targeted investigations. Severity is staged by size (palpable, visible, >4 cm) and by functional status (euthyroid, hyper, hypo).

t.b: Is the gland over‑ or under‑producing hormone? Low TSH = hyperthyroidism; high TSH = hypothyroidism
Helps monitor differentiated thyroid cancer; not routinely available, use clinical follow‑up instead
Distinguishes solid vs cystic nodules, assesses size and vascularity; if unavailable, rely on palpation and clinical suspicion
Detects malignancy in nodules >1 cm or suspicious features; if not possible, refer for surgical assessment

b: Thyrotoxic crisis → beta‑blocker and antithyroid therapy
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals the most urgent tasks are to identify life‑threatening hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxic crisis) and to rule out compressive symptoms that may compromise airway or cause venous congestion.

t.b: Detects bruit or thrill suggesting Graves disease; if present, prioritize antithyroid treatment
Identifies hypocalcaemia risk after thyroidectomy; if unavailable, monitor for tetany clinically

b: Always comment on size, consistency, mobility and presence of bruit
Link iodine deficiency to endemic regions and dietary habits
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to integrate history, exam and limited investigations, and to prioritize management in resource‑constrained settings.

b: Neglecting to ask about goitrogenic foods (cassava, millet) and herbal remedies
Over‑reliance on ultrasound when not available
sections.p: Students often list causes without prioritising likely local aetiologies, forget to assess thyroid function, or assume all nodules are malignant.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in size with dysphagia or stridor
Signs of thyrotoxic crisis (fever, tachycardia, agitation)
Neck pain with fever suggesting suppurative thyroiditis
